docs.text: UltraGPS Arduino Firmware ¶ Arduino firmware for the St. Mary's University UltraGPS positioning system, developed as part of graduate research. The repository holds the two Arduino scripts that run on the Arduino Uno's that are the physical backbone of the system. The base station accepts single-letter commands over USB serial, tells the transmitter over a 2.4 GHz radio link when to fire, times the ultrasonic echoes returned by six receivers, and prints the resulting tick counts back over serial. The transmitter station listens for those radio packets, keeps its timer phase-locked to the base station, and drives the ultrasonic transmitter. The base station is the board that the UltraGPS Ground Station program ( UltraGpsXY ) talks to over USB serial. Documentation ¶ Architecture — how the two sketches are structured and how a measurement flows through the system. Hardware — boards, wiring, and the full pin map for both stations. Installation — installing the toolchain (PlatformIO or arduino-cli ) and getting the sources. Uploading — flashing each sketch onto the right board. Configuration — every compile-time setting and where it lives. Usage — the serial command set and the output format. Developer's Guide — a self-contained reference for anyone forking the repository At a glance ¶ Sketches base-station/ , transmitter-station/ Board Arduino Uno (ATmega328P, 16 MHz) Framework Arduino, built with PlatformIO ( platform = atmelavr ) Depedency nRF24/RF24 (pulled in automatically) Serial 38400 bps, 8N1 Radio nRF24L01+, channel 100, 1 Mbps, 8-byte fixed payload Pulse rate 10 Hz (Timer1, CTC mode) Receivers 6, on A0 – A5 Quick start ¶ Every release ships prebuilt .hex images and a zip of the sketch sources on the Releases page . You do not need a toolchain to flash a release — arduino-cli alone will do it: arduino-cli upload -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b arduino:avr:uno \ --input-file ultragps-base-station-v1.0.hex To build from source instead, see Installation and Uploading .

docs.text: Architecture ¶ The repository contains two independent PlatformIO projects , one per Arduino. They share four source files by copy ( radio , led_control , timers , debug_macros ) Projects ¶ Project Runs on Responsibility base-station/ Arduino Uno wired to the six receivers Serial command interface, radio master, echo timing, serial output transmitter-station/ Arduino Uno wired to the ultrasonic transmitter Radio slave, PLL phase correction, fires the ultrasonic trigger The transmitter station is the radio receiver Modules ¶ Both sketches are organised the same way: a setup() / loop() control file plus a small set of single-purpose modules. Module Files Responsibility Control main.cpp Pin/module setup, command callbacks, main loop Radio radio.{h,cpp} nRF24L01+ setup, CommsPacket framing, send/receive Timers timers.{h,cpp} Timer1 CTC setup, the TIMER1_COMPA ISR, PLL correction LEDs led_control.{h,cpp} Status LED state, startup animation Debug debug_macros.h Compile-time-gated DEBUG_* / DEBUG_INFO_* printing Commands command_control.{h,cpp} Serial line buffering and command dispatch ( base station only ) Third-party library ¶ nRF24/RF24 is declared in each platformio.ini as lib_deps and is downloaded into .pio/libdeps/ on the first build. Data flow ¶ Ground station PC (UltraGpsXY) │ (USB serial, /dev/ttyACM0 @ 38400) │ commands: P / S / C data: "N: t0, ..., t5" ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BASE STATION │ │ CommandControl ──► handleUltrasonics() │ │ │ ▲ │ │ RadioController measure_echo_times │ └────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘ │ nRF24 CommsPacket ▲ echoes on A0–A5 │ (TCNT1, tick_delay) │ ▼ │ ┌────────────────────┐ │ │ TRANSMITTER STATION│ │ │ IRQ ► pllCorrect()│ │ │ Timer1 ISR ► pin 5│ │ └────────┬───────────┘ │ │ trigger pulse │ ▼ │ Ultrasonic transmitter ═══► 6 receivers ──┘ (sound) How one measurement happens ¶ The base station receives a command byte ( P , S , or C ) over serial. CommandControl::poll() buffers the line and dispatches to the callback in the global command table. handleUltrasonics() clears trigger_fired and calls RadioController::sendTrigger(TCNT1, SONIC_BURST_DELAY) . The packet carries the base station's current Timer1 count and a µs delay. The transmitter station's radio raises its IRQ line. onRadioIRQ() reads the packet and calls pllCorrect(timer_val - TCNT1) , nudging the local Timer1 so the two boards stay in phase, and stores the tick delay. Both boards' Timer1 reach compare-match. Each TIMER1_COMPA_vect ISR pulses its trigger pin (pin 5) for 50 µs and sets trigger_fired . On the transmitter that pulse fires the ultrasonic burst, while on the receiver it triggers the receive functionality of the receivers. The base station, released from its while(!trigger_fired) wait, runs measure_echo_times() . It polls PINC & 63 in a tight loop for up to some amount of (~60 at the time of writing) ms, recording every change of the six echo lines along with the loop iteration count at which it changed. The recorded transitions are reduced to one tick count per receiver, and the six values are printed over serial as one comma-separated line. Timing model ¶ Everything is driven by Timer1 in CTC mode with a prescaler of 256 , so one timer tick is 16 µs. timers.cpp provides four rates: Function OCR1A Rate timer1_init_5Hz() 12498 5 Hz timer1_init_10Hz() 6249 10 Hz (default on both boards) timer1_init_15Hz() 4166 ≈ 14.999 Hz timer1_init_20Hz() 3124 20 Hz The two boards free-run at the same nominal rate; the radio packet is what keeps them aligned. Because the packet carries the base station's raw TCNT1 , the transmitter can compute its phase error directly and add it to its own TCNT1 — a one-step software PLL, implemented as pllCorrect() in timers.h . Ticks are not the same as Timer1 counts: The values printed over serial are loop iterations of the sampling loop in measure_echo_times() , are not Timer1 ticks. They carry an Ax + B type relationship to distance: A converts counts to time/distance and B absorbs the fact that counting does not begin exactly at zero. Calibration is done downstream, not on the Arduino. Logging ¶ Serial printing is gated at compile time by two macros in debug_macros.h : INFO_DEBUG — activates the DEBUG_INFO_* macros (status and error messages: radio init, trigger fired, packet failures). DEBUG — activates both DEBUG_INFO_* and the verbose DEBUG_* macros (tick counts, PINC values, sampling diagnostics). Neither is defined by default, so both sets compile away to nothing. Plain Serial.println() calls — the measurement output and the base station's fatal radio error — are always present. See Configuration .

docs.text: Configuration ¶ All configuration are compile-time , which means that any change in these settings will need to be re-uploaded to the board. Where each setting lives ¶ File Controls <project>/platformio.ini Board, serial ports, monitor baud, libraries <project>/src/main.cpp Baud rate, pin assignments, command table, sampling window, simulation <project>/src/timers.cpp Pulse rate, trigger pin, trigger pulse width <project>/src/command_control.h Continuous-mode rate, command buffer limits (base station only) <project>/src/radio.{h,cpp} Radio channel, data rate, power, pipe addresses <project>/src/debug_macros.h Debug output level Some settings must be changed on both boards The baud rate, pulse rate, and radio parameters exist independently in each project. Change one and the boards stop agreeing. Each entry below says whether it needs to be kept in sync. PlatformIO project settings ¶ base-station/platformio.ini : [env:uno] platform = atmelavr board = uno framework = arduino lib_deps = nRF24/RF24 monitor_speed = 38400 monitor_port = /dev/ttyACM0 upload_port = /dev/ttyACM0 Key Default (base / transmitter) Notes board uno Change for a different AVR board. The PINC reads and Timer1 values assume an ATmega328P at 16 MHz. lib_deps nRF24/RF24 Downloaded on first build monitor_speed 38400 Must match BAUD_RATE in main.cpp monitor_port /dev/ttyACM0 / /dev/ttyACM1 Port the serial monitor opens upload_port /dev/ttyACM0 / /dev/ttyACM1 Port --target upload flashes Override the upload port for a single run instead of editing the file: pio run -d base-station --target upload --upload-port /dev/ttyACM2 Serial ¶ Setting File Default Notes BAUD_RATE main.cpp (both) 38400 Keep in sync across both sketches, both platformio.ini files, and the ground-station program's --baud-rate CMD_BUF_SIZE command_control.h 64 Longest accepted command line, including the NUL. Longer lines are discarded, not truncated. CMD_MAX_ARGS command_control.h 4 Maximum arguments any one command can carry Pulse rate ¶ Both boards call a timer1_init_*() function from setup() . timers.cpp provides four; the default on both is 10 Hz: timer1_init_10Hz(); // in setup(), base-station and transmitter-station Function Rate OCR1A value timer1_init_5Hz() 5 Hz 12498 timer1_init_10Hz() 10 Hz 6249 timer1_init_15Hz() ≈ 14.999 Hz 4166 timer1_init_20Hz() 20 Hz 3124 Change this on both boards. The PLL corrects phase, not frequency — if the boards run at different rates the transmitter is yanked back into phase every packet and the timing is unusable. All four use CTC mode with a prescaler of 256, so one tick is 16 µs. To add a rate, copy one of the functions and set OCR1A = 16000000 / 256 / f - 1 , then assign the same value to timer1_top . Faster is not always better The sampling window in measure_echo_times() is capped at 80 % of timer1_top , so raising the rate shortens the window and reduces the maximum measurable range. At 20 Hz the window is roughly half of what it is at 10 Hz. Trigger timing ¶ Setting File Default Meaning triggerPin timers.cpp (both) 5 Pin pulsed by the Timer1 ISR TRIGGER_PULSE_US timers.cpp (both) 50 Trigger pulse width. The HC-SR04 datasheet requires 10 µs; 50 µs is a safety margin. SONIC_BURST_DELAY main.cpp (base, inside handleUltrasonics() ) 2*1000 Microseconds the transmitter waits after the packet before firing, giving the receivers time to settle into receive mode SYNC_PLL_INTERVAL main.cpp (base) 10 Milliseconds between PLL sync packets tick_delay timers.cpp (transmitter) set by radio Applied as delayMicroseconds() at the top of the ISR. Hard-capped at 16383 µs by delayMicroseconds() . Sampling window ¶ Inside measure_echo_times() : constexpr long max_tick_val = 0x31000/4; //! About 60 ms of sampling time 50 176 iterations of the polling loop, whichever comes first with the 80 % timer cut-off. Raising it extends the maximum measurable distance; it cannot usefully exceed the pulse period. The transition buffers are fixed at 100 entries: static byte value[100]; static unsigned long ticks[100]; Sampling stops early if all 100 fill up. With six receivers and one rising plus one falling edge each, 100 is generous — but a noisy echo line can burn through it and truncate the measurement. Radio ¶ Set in RadioController::init() in radio.cpp , and identical on both boards apart from the pipe direction. Every one of these must match on both boards. Setting Default Notes setChannel(100) 100 0–125. Change on both boards to dodge Wi-Fi interference. setDataRate(RF24_1MBPS) 1 Mbps RF24_250KBPS gives more range at the cost of latency setPALevel(RF24_PA_HIGH) HIGH Drop to RF24_PA_LOW if the modules are close and the supply is marginal setPayloadSize(8) 8 Must equal sizeof(CommsPacket) setAutoAck(false) off Deliberate — a retried trigger would arrive too late to be useful setRetries(0, 0) none Same reason PIPE_TX_TO_RX 0xF0F0F0F0E1 Base → transmitter. Change on both boards if two UltraGPS systems share a room. PIPE_RX_TO_TX 0xF0F0F0F0E2 Opened both ways but currently unused Radio pins are set where the controller is constructed in main.cpp : RadioController radioCtrl(9, 10); //! CE, CSN constexpr uint8_t radioIRQPin = 2; //! transmitter only; must be pin 2 or 3 LEDs ¶ LedControl leds(3, 4, 6, 7, 8); //! STAT_1, STAT_2, STAT_3, PULSE_TRIG, RADIO_STATUS Both sketches call leds.init(0) in setup() , which skips the startup animation. Change it to leds.init(1) to run the ~2.5 s LED chase on every reset. Debug output ¶ debug_macros.h (a separate copy per project) gates all diagnostic printing: //! Enable debug mode //#define DEBUG Macro Uncomment to get (neither) Default. Only measurement output and fatal radio errors are printed. INFO_DEBUG DEBUG_INFO_* messages: radio init, packet send failures, trigger-fired notices DEBUG Both sets — adds DEBUG_* verbose diagnostics ( nwp , highest tick, max PINC value) Debug output corrupts the data stream Diagnostics go to the same serial port as the measurements, so a program parsing the output — such as the ground-station UltraGpsXY — will see interleaved lines it cannot decode. Enable these only when driving the board from a human-readable serial monitor. Simulation mode ¶ The base station can produce plausible fake tick counts without any working ultrasonic hardware, which is the fastest way to test the serial link and any program consuming it. There are two ways in: The S command — always available. Runs the real radio and trigger path but prints simulated values instead of measured ones. The SIMULATE_REAL_COMMANDS macro — at the top of base-station/src/main.cpp : //! Definition to simulate "real" commands with pulse data //#define SIMULATE_REAL_COMMANDS Uncomment it to make P and C behave like S too, so every command returns simulated data. Use this when the consuming program only issues P and C and you do not want to modify it. Simulated values come from simulate_echo_times() : a base of 401 counts with a ±50 deterministic variation per receiver that shifts on each call. constexpr unsigned long BASE_COUNT = 401; constexpr int VARIATION = 50; Simulation still needs the radio onSimulatePulse() calls handleUltrasonics(false) before faking the numbers, so the radio must still initialise or the sketch halts in setup() . It does not need the ultrasonic hardware or the receivers.

docs.text: Developer's Guide ¶ A self-contained reference for developers who fork the repository and need to work with the project's tooling — building, flashing, previewing the documentation, extending the firmware, and cutting releases. Everything needed is on this page. Overview ¶ The repository holds two Arduino sketches, one per microcontroller in the UltraGPS positioning system: base-station/ — accepts single-letter commands over USB serial, sends the trigger packet over the nRF24L01+ link, times the echoes returned by six ultrasonic receivers on A0 – A5 , and prints the counts back over serial. This is the board the ground-station program ( UltraGpsXY ) talks to. transmitter-station/ — listens for those radio packets, corrects its Timer1 phase to match the base station, and pulses the ultrasonic transmitter's trigger pin. Requirements ¶ PlatformIO Core ( pio ) with Python 3 — builds and flashes the firmware arduino-cli — optional, for flashing loose .hex files git — to clone the repository (no submodules) Python 3 with pip — only needed to build/preview the documentation git clone https://github.com/Imperious22M/UltraGPS-Arduino.git cd UltraGPS-Arduino python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/platformio ~/.venvs/platformio/bin/pip install platformio export PATH="$HOME/.venvs/platformio/bin:$PATH" Flashing a prebuilt release ¶ You do not need a build toolchain to run the firmware — each release ships prebuilt .hex images. Download them from the Releases page and flash with arduino-cli : arduino-cli upload -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b arduino:avr:uno \ --input-file ultragps-base-station-v1.0.hex Using the build script ¶ build.sh is the single entry point for building, flashing, cleaning, packaging, and previewing the docs. docs.text: The repository holds two Arduino sketches, one per microcontroller in the UltraGPS positioning system: base-station/ — accepts single-letter commands over USB serial, sends the trigger packet over the nRF24L01+ link, times the echoes returned by six ultrasonic receivers on A0 – A5 , and prints the counts back over serial. docs.text: Hardware ¶ Both stations are Arduino Unos (ATmega328P at 16 MHz) with an nRF24L01+ radio module and five status LEDs. The pin assignments are identical apart from the radio IRQ line, which only the transmitter station uses. Bill of materials ¶ Item Qty Notes Arduino Uno 2 One per station nRF24L01+ radio module 2 2.4 GHz, SPI HC-SR04-style ultrasonic transmitter 1 Driven by the transmitter station Ultrasonic receivers 6 Echo lines feed the base station's A0 – A5 Status LEDs (+ resistors, optional) 10 Five per station Power the radio properly The nRF24L01+ draws current in bursts that the Uno's 3.3 V regulator handles poorly. A 10 µF capacitor across the module's VCC / GND is the usual fix for radio.begin() succeeding but packets failing intermittently. Pin map — base station ¶ Defined in base-station/src/main.cpp and base-station/src/timers.cpp . Pin Direction Signal Set in 2 — Radio IRQ — declared but unused main.cpp ( radioIRQPin ) 3 OUT STAT_1 LED LedControl leds(3, 4, 6, 7, 8) 4 OUT STAT_2 LED " 5 OUT Trigger pulse (50 µs, fired by the Timer1 ISR) timers.cpp ( triggerPin ) 6 OUT STAT_3 LED LedControl 7 OUT PULSE_TRIG LED — lit while a pulse is in flight " 8 OUT RADIO_STATUS LED — solid once the radio initialises " 9 OUT Radio CE RadioController radioCtrl(9, 10) 10 OUT Radio CSN " 11 OUT SPI MOSI → radio Hardware SPI 12 IN SPI MISO ← radio " 13 OUT SPI SCK → radio " A0 – A5 IN (pull-up) Echo lines from receivers 0–5 ECHO_PIN[] The six echo lines must stay on A0 – A5 : measure_echo_times() reads them as a group with PINC & 63 , which is a direct read of PORTC 's low six bits. Moving a receiver to a digital pin would silently drop it from the measurement. Pin map — transmitter station ¶ Defined in transmitter-station/src/main.cpp and transmitter-station/src/timers.cpp . Pin Direction Signal 2 IN Radio IRQ — attachInterrupt(..., FALLING) drives onRadioIRQ() 3 OUT STAT_1 LED 4 OUT STAT_2 LED 5 OUT Trigger to the ultrasonic transmitter (50 µs pulse) 6 OUT STAT_3 LED 7 OUT PULSE_TRIG LED 8 OUT RADIO_STATUS LED 9 OUT Radio CE 10 OUT Radio CSN 11 – 13 IN/OUT Hardware SPI to the radio Pin 2 must be interrupt-capable. Radio link ¶ Both stations configure the nRF24L01+ identically in RadioController::init() , except for which pipe they write to: Setting Value Channel 100 Data rate RF24_1MBPS PA level RF24_PA_HIGH Payload 8 bytes, fixed (dynamic payloads disabled) Auto-ack Off Retries setRetries(0, 0) — none Base station writes to PIPE_TX_TO_RX ( 0xF0F0F0F0E1 ) Transmitter listens on PIPE_TX_TO_RX , writes to PIPE_RX_TO_TX ( 0xF0F0F0F0E2 ) Auto-ack and retries are deliberately off: a late trigger packet is worse than a lost one, so the link is fire-and-forget. The 8-byte payload is CommsPacket ( radio.h ): Field Type Meaning type PacketType PKT_NO_DATA (1) or PKT_TRIGGER (2) _pad[3] uint8_t Alignment padding to keep the struct at 8 bytes timestamp uint16_t The base station's TCNT1 at send time tick_delay uint16_t Microseconds the transmitter waits before firing Status LEDs ¶ LedControl drives all five LEDs on each board and holds a shadow copy of their state, so getStat1() and friends never need a digitalRead on an output pin. LED Meaning RADIO_STATUS (pin 8) Solid once the radio initialises. Blinking on a two-second cycle means radio init failed and the sketch has halted. PULSE_TRIG (pin 7) Lit while a trigger is in active STAT_1 – STAT_3 (pins 3, 4, 6) Reserved — wired and controllable, but nothing currently drives them Both sketches call leds.init(0) , which sets the pins to output and drives them low without the startup animation. Pass leds.init(1) (or omit the argument) to run startupAnimation() — a chase pattern across all five LEDs, useful as a quick "the board rebooted" indicator.

docs.text: Installation ¶ There are two ways to get firmware onto a board: flash a prebuilt .hex from a release, or build the sketches from source. Flashing a release needs no build toolchain at all. Flash from a release (recommended) ¶ Each tagged version is published on the Releases page with three assets attached: Asset What it is ultragps-base-station-vX.Y.hex Prebuilt base-station firmware ultragps-transmitter-station-vX.Y.hex Prebuilt transmitter-station firmware ultragps-arduino-sources-vX.Y.zip The Arduino sketches and their PlatformIO project files Download the two .hex files and flash them with arduino-cli : arduino-cli upload -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b arduino:avr:uno \ --input-file ultragps-base-station-v1.0.hex arduino-cli upload -p /dev/ttyACM1 -b arduino:avr:uno \ --input-file ultragps-transmitter-station-v1.0.hex Take care to send each image to the right board — see Uploading for how to tell them apart, and Configuration if you need to change a setting (which does require building from source). Prerequisites for building from source ¶ PlatformIO Core ( pio ) — the primary toolchain; each project is a PlatformIO project. Needs Python 3. arduino-cli — optional, only needed for the base-station/upload helper script and for flashing loose .hex files. git — to clone the repository. The AVR compiler toolchain and the RF24 library are downloaded automatically by PlatformIO on the first build. Installing PlatformIO Core ¶ python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/platformio ~/.venvs/platformio/bin/pip install platformio # Optional: put `pio` on your PATH export PATH="$HOME/.venvs/platformio/bin:$PATH" The official installer script is an alternative: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/platformio/platformio-core-installer/master/get-platformio.py -o get-platformio.py python3 get-platformio.py Installing arduino-cli ¶ curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arduino/arduino-cli/master/install.sh | sh arduino-cli core install arduino:avr Serial port permissions (Linux) ¶ The Arduino's usually appears as /dev/ttyACM<some number> Your user must be in the dialout group to open it: sudo usermod -aG dialout "$USER" Log out and back in for the group change to take effect. Get the sources ¶ git clone https://github.com/Imperious22M/UltraGPS-Arduino.git cd UltraGPS-Arduino Build ¶ Each station is built separately with pio run -d <project> : pio run -d base-station pio run -d transmitter-station The first build takes a couple of minutes while PlatformIO downloads the atmelavr platform and the RF24 library; later builds take seconds. Each project's artefacts land in <project>/.pio/build/uno/ , with the flashable image at firmware.hex . To clean: pio run -d base-station --target clean

docs.text: Notes ¶ Design notes, gotchas, and open items. "Transmitter station" is the radio receiver ¶ The naming is inverted depending on which link you look at. transmitter-station/src/main.cpp opens with "Receiver program for the UltraGPS system" and its RadioController::init() defaults to as_receiver = true . Both are correct: the board receives on the radio link and transmits on the ultrasonic one. The directory name follows the ultrasonic role; the source comments follow the radio role. The shared modules are copies, and they have drifted ¶ radio.* , timers.* , led_control.* , and debug_macros.h exist separately in each project rather than in a shared library directory. led_control.* and debug_macros.h are still byte-identical, but the other two have diverged: File Difference radio.cpp The base station calls maskIRQ(true, true, false) (IRQ on RX only); the transmitter does not. The pipes are opened in opposite directions, as they must be. timers.h/.cpp pllCorrect() takes a second tick_delay argument on the base station and one argument on the transmitter. Only the transmitter's ISR applies tick_delay before pulsing. A fix applied to one copy does not reach the other. Consolidating them into a PlatformIO lib/ directory shared by both projects would remove the hazard, but it is not done today. Interval timers in loop() are reset every iteration ¶ base-station/src/main.cpp declares its interval bookkeeping inside loop() : void loop() { long currentTime = millis(); long lastSyncTime = 0; long lastPulseTime = 0; ... if (millis() - lastSyncTime >= (unsigned int)SYNC_PLL_INTERVAL) { ... } Because lastSyncTime and lastPulseTime are re-initialised to 0 on every pass, both comparisons are true on every pass once the board has been up for a few milliseconds. In practice: syncPLL() sends a packet on every loop iteration , not every 10 ms as SYNC_PLL_INTERVAL suggests. In continuous mode, continuousPollingDelay (20 ms) has no effect. The real rate limit is the blocking while(!trigger_fired){} wait inside handleUltrasonics() , which ties output to the Timer1 rate — about 10 lines per second at the default 10 Hz. Making the constants meaningful means declaring the two variables static (or moving them to file scope). Doing so would change the observed radio traffic and the continuous-mode rate, so it is a behavioural change, not a pure cleanup. measure_echo_times() is called with interrupts enabled ¶ The call site reads: //! Measure the echo times without interrupts to avoid timing issues with the radio IRQ measure_echo_times(false); The comment describes the opposite of what the argument does — false means noInterrupts() is not called, so interrupts stay enabled during sampling. The function supports both; only the comment is stale. Passing true would block the Timer1 ISR for the duration of the sampling window, which is why the enabled path is the one in use. The measurement is hard-wired to six receivers on PORTC ¶ echo_value() is PINC & 63 — a single read of the low six bits of PORTC , which is what makes it fast enough to sample all six channels in one tight loop. The consequence is that ECHO_PIN[] , the this_ticks[6] arrays, and the print statement in handleUltrasonics() cannot be re-pointed by editing the array alone. Fewer than six receivers works — unused pins stay pulled up and report 0 — but more than six, or receivers on digital pins, needs the measurement and printing code changed too. The transition buffers value[100] and ticks[100] account for 500 of the 923 bytes of RAM the base station uses. Sampling stops early if they fill. Half-built features ¶ Several constants and code paths are present but inert. They are not dead code so much as unfinished work: tick_delay on the base station. TRIGGER_TICK_DELAY (100 ticks) is declared but never sent; handleUltrasonics() passes a hard-coded SONIC_BURST_DELAY of 2000 µs instead. The transmitter honours whatever arrives. syncPLL() . It sends a trigger packet with tick_delay = 0 , with the intent of nudging the transmitter's PLL without firing the ultrasonic burst. The transmitter has no way to distinguish this from a real trigger, so it fires anyway. The source marks it TODO … NOT YET IMPLEMENTED and adds "MAY NOT EVER BE IMPLEMENTED" . LATENCY_COMPENSATION_US (4000 µs, radio.h , both projects) is declared and never read. docs.text: The naming is inverted depending on which link you look at. transmitter-station/src/main.cpp opens with "Receiver program for the UltraGPS system" and its RadioController::init() defaults to as_receiver = true . docs.text: radio.* , timers.* , led_control.* , and debug_macros.h exist separately in each project rather than in a shared library directory. led_control.* and debug_macros.h are still byte-identical, but the other two have diverged: File Difference radio.cpp The base station calls maskIRQ(true, true, false) (IRQ on RX only); the transmitter does not. docs.text: base-station/src/main.cpp declares its interval bookkeeping inside loop() : void loop() { long currentTime = millis(); long lastSyncTime = 0; long lastPulseTime = 0; ... if (millis() - lastSyncTime >= (unsigned int)SYNC_PLL_INTERVAL) { ... } Because lastSyncTime and lastPulseTime are re-initialised to 0 on every pass, both comparisons are true on every pass once the board has been up for a few milliseconds. In practice: syncPLL() sends a packet on every loop iteration , not every 10 ms as SYNC_PLL_INTERVAL suggests. In continuous mode, continuousPollingDelay (20 ms) has no effect. The real rate limit is the blocking while(!trigger_fired){} wait inside handleUltrasonics() , which ties output to the Timer1 rate — about 10 lines per second at the default 10 Hz. Making the constants meaningful means declaring the two variables static (or moving them to file scope). Doing so would change the observed radio traffic and the continuous-mode rate, so it is a behavioural change, not a pure cleanup.
docs.title: Interval timers in loop() are reset every iteration

docs.text: The call site reads: //! Measure the echo times without interrupts to avoid timing issues with the radio IRQ measure_echo_times(false); The comment describes the opposite of what the argument does — false means noInterrupts() is not called, so interrupts stay enabled during sampling. The function supports both; only the comment is stale. Passing true would block the Timer1 ISR for the duration of the sampling window, which is why the enabled path is the one in use.
docs.title: measure_echo_times() is called with interrupts enabled

docs.text: echo_value() is PINC & 63 — a single read of the low six bits of PORTC , which is what makes it fast enough to sample all six channels in one tight loop. The consequence is that ECHO_PIN[] , the this_ticks[6] arrays, and the print statement in handleUltrasonics() cannot be re-pointed by editing the array alone. Fewer than six receivers works — unused pins stay pulled up and report 0 — but more than six, or receivers on digital pins, needs the measurement and printing code changed too. The transition buffers value[100] and ticks[100] account for 500 of the 923 bytes of RAM the base station uses. Sampling stops early if they fill.

docs.text: Uploading ¶ Flashing a sketch means picking the right project and the right serial port. The two boards are identical Arduino Unos, so nothing prevents the base-station firmware from being flashed on the transmitter board. Identify the boards ¶ Listing everything currently attached: arduino-cli board list Example output: Port Protocol Type Board Name FQBN Core /dev/ttyACM0 serial Serial Port (USB) Arduino Uno arduino:avr:uno arduino:avr /dev/ttyACM1 serial Serial Port (USB) Arduino Uno arduino:avr:uno arduino:avr PlatformIO can do the same: pio device list Ports are assigned in the order the boards are plugged in, not by role, so /dev/ttyACM0 is not permanently the base station . If unsure which is which, unplug one and re-run the command. The repository's defaults assume: Project Default port base-station /dev/ttyACM0 transmitter-station /dev/ttyACM1 Those defaults live in each project's platformio.ini — change them if the boards enumerate differently (see Configuration ). Upload with PlatformIO (recommended) ¶ From the repository root: pio run -d base-station --target upload pio run -d transmitter-station --target upload This compiles and flashes in one step, using the upload_port from that project's platformio.ini . To override the port for a single run: pio run -d base-station --target upload --upload-port /dev/ttyACM1 A successful upload ends with [SUCCESS] and an avrdude verification line. Upload with arduino-cli ¶ arduino-cli can build and flash the PlatformIO source tree directly, because the sketches are plain C++ under src/ : arduino-cli compile --upload -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b arduino:avr:uno base-station/src To flash a prebuilt .hex from a release without compiling anything: arduino-cli upload -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b arduino:avr:uno \ --input-file ultragps-base-station-v1.0.hex Troubleshooting ¶ Symptom Likely cause Permission denied: /dev/ttyACM0 Your user is not in the dialout group — see Installation avrdude: stk500_recv(): programmer is not responding Wrong port, or a serial monitor still holds the port open. Close it and retry. RADIO_STATUS blinks slowly and never goes solid radio.begin() or isChipConnected() failed — check the nRF24 wiring and its power supply Upload succeeds, serial prints nothing Monitor is at the wrong baud rate; the sketches use 38400 P returns all zeros The transmitter station is not firing — confirm it is powered, flashed, and its radio LED is solid Garbled serial output Baud mismatch, or DEBUG was left enabled in debug_macros.h and is interleaving diagnostics with data

docs.text: Usage ¶ Only the base station has a user interface. It listens on USB serial at 38400 bps and responds to single-letter commands. The transmitter station has no command interface — once flashed it runs autonomously, reacting to radio packets and its own timer. Connecting ¶ Any 38400 bps serial terminal works: pio device monitor -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b 38400 screen /dev/ttyACM0 38400 # exit with Ctrl-A then k Opening the port asserts DTR, which resets the Uno. setup() waits up to 3 seconds for the host to attach, so give it a moment before sending the first command. In normal operation the port is held by the ground-station program ( UltraGpsXY ), which issues these same commands on behalf of network clients. Only one program can hold the port at a time. Commands ¶ Send one letter followed by a newline or carriage return. Anything else is silently discarded. Command Effect Response P Fire one pulse and measure the echoes. Leaves (or returns to) polling mode. One N: line C Enter continuous mode — measure and report repeatedly until interrupted A stream of C: lines S Fire one pulse but report simulated counts. Returns to polling mode. One N: line Line endings matter CommandControl::poll() only dispatches a command when it sees \n or \r . In the Arduino IDE's Serial Monitor, set the line-ending dropdown to Newline or Carriage return — with No line ending nothing will ever happen. Leaving continuous mode ¶ There is no stop command. Send P or S — both set the polling state back to POLLING , which ends the stream. Resetting the board works too. Invalid input ¶ Unknown letters, empty lines, and lines longer than 63 characters are dropped without any response. The base station never echoes input and never reports an error for a bad command, so silence after a command means it was not recognised. Output format ¶ Every measurement is one line: a two-character mode marker, then six comma-separated ticks, one per receiver, in A0 – A5 order. N: 4404, 3226, 4063, 4041, 3133, 4109 C: 4398, 3231, 4059, 4044, 3130, 4112 Marker Meaning N: Normal — a single measurement, from P or S C: Continuous — part of the stream started by C The marker exists so a consuming program can tell solicited replies from streamed data on the same port. What the numbers mean ¶ Each value is the number of sampling-loop iterations between the trigger and that receiver's echo going low — a tick , not microseconds and not millimetres. Converting to distance takes the form Ax + B , where A scales counts to time or distance and B absorbs the fact that counting does not start at exactly zero. Both constants are determined by calibration downstream; the firmware does no conversion. A value of 0 means that receiver never produced a usable echo transition within the sampling window — out of range, not wired, or the pulse never fired. Example session ¶ $ pio device monitor -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b 38400 P N: 4404, 3226, 4063, 4041, 3133, 4109 P N: 4401, 3229, 4066, 4038, 3135, 4106 C C: 4400, 3227, 4064, 4040, 3134, 4108 C: 4399, 3230, 4062, 4043, 3131, 4110 C: 4402, 3228, 4065, 4039, 3136, 4107 P N: 4403, 3227, 4063, 4041, 3133, 4109 Rates ¶ In continuous mode loop() checks continuousPollingDelay (20 ms) before starting the next measurement, but each measurement blocks in handleUltrasonics() waiting for the next Timer1 compare match. The trigger rate is therefore the real limit: at the default 10 Hz you get about ten lines per second regardless of the 20 ms constant. Raising the output rate means changing the timer rate on both boards — see Configuration . Startup behaviour ¶ On reset the base station: Opens the serial port at 38400 and waits up to 3 s for the host. Sets A0 – A5 to INPUT_PULLUP . Initialises the LEDs (animation off by default). Starts Timer1 at 10 Hz. Initialises the radio. If this fails the sketch halts , blinking RADIO_STATUS on a two-second cycle (1 s on, 1 s off) and printing [ERROR] Still halted. on each cycle. Nothing recovers this except fixing the wiring and resetting the board. Leaves RADIO_STATUS solid and waits for commands. There is no banner or ready message on a successful start — the first output you see is the response to your first command.
